title: Taming Rogue AI Agents with Observability-Driven Evaluation — Jim Bennett, Galileo

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core focus is evaluation methodology—LLM-as-judge, step-level metrics, and integrating evals throughout the lifecycle. The framework applies across verticals and is delivered as a developer-platform talk from Galileo. The speaker explicitly covers design-time metric definition, development-phase prompt/model selection, CI/CD testing, and production observation with alerting. Conference audience assumed to have AI/LLM background, but concepts are explained accessibly without deep implementation detail. Recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer World's Fair with slides and a fintech chatbot demo. Eleven transcript evidence anchors directly support evaluation methodology as the primary focus.

summary: Jim Bennett, Principal Developer Advocate at Galileo, addresses the challenge of detecting, diagnosing, and correcting failures in AI agents at production scale. He begins by highlighting the trust deficit in AI, citing real-world failures: the Chicago Sun Times publishing an AI-generated summer reading list with hallucinated books, a law firm citing non-existent case law, and Air Canada's chatbot making legally binding promises. These examples underscore that AI is non-deterministic, making traditional unit testing inadequate. Bennett introduces the principle of 'set a thief to catch a thief': using LLMs to evaluate AI applications, noting that AIs perform roughly as well as humans at judging whether AI output is correct. He recommends using a better or more capable LLM for evaluation than the one used in production, and mentions Galileo's custom-trained evaluation model. He demonstrates with a fintech chatbot where querying account balance requires multiple turns, highlighting the need for granular, step-level evaluation rather than binary pass/fail. He introduces action completion (did the flow achieve its end goal?) and action advancement (did it move forward?) as distinct metrics, showing how traces broken down by individual steps with red/green indicators enable precise diagnosis. Bennett then describes how AI can analyze the unstructured evaluation data to generate smart insights and suggested fixes—for example, recommending explicit system message instructions so the bot retrieves all account balances. He stresses that fixes should not be applied automatically, emphasizing the importance of human-in-the-loop review and continuous learning by human feedback (CLHF), since metrics are never perfect out of the box and require ongoing training. He closes with a step-by-step recap: add evaluations from the start, define precise metrics at design time (toxicity, hallucinations, RAG quality, custom use-case measures), carry evaluations through production since users behave unpredictably, and implement real-time alerting so teams are notified when agents go rogue. He invites attendees to visit the Galileo booth and sign up for their free offering.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: AI is non-deterministic, making traditional unit testing inadequate for multi-step agentic workflows
Use AI (LLMs) to evaluate AI ('set a thief to catch a thief')—AI judges perform comparably to humans at this task
Use a better or more capable LLM for evaluation than the one used in production to ensure quality assessment
Evaluate at granular, step-level detail—not just binary pass/fail across the whole flow
Action completion and action advancement are distinct metrics: completion measures end-goal achievement, advancement measures forward progress
AI can analyze unstructured evaluation data to generate insights and suggest fixes, but humans must remain in the loop to review and approve changes
Metrics are never perfect out of the box; they require continuous training via human feedback (CLHF)
Define precise metrics at design time—covering toxicity, hallucinations, RAG quality, comprehensibility, and custom use-case needs—and carry them through production
Implement real-time alerting so teams are notified immediately when AI agents go rogue in production
Integrate evaluations from day one—during prompt engineering, model selection, CI/CD pipelines, and production observation

sections.title: Introduction and the Trust Problem in AI
sections.summary: Bennett introduces the topic of taming rogue AI agents and asks the audience who uses and trusts AI, establishing that trust in AI is very low.

sections.title: Real-World AI Failure Examples
sections.summary: Cites the Chicago Sun Times publishing an AI-hallucinated summer reading list, a law firm citing false case law, and Air Canada's chatbot as examples of AI failures eroding trust.

sections.title: The Challenge of Testing Non-Deterministic AI
sections.summary: Explains why traditional unit testing fails for AI: non-deterministic outputs, complex agentic workflows with multiple LLM/agent/tool calls, and the difficulty of defining what 'working' even means.

sections.title: Set a Thief to Catch a Thief: AI Evaluating AI
sections.summary: Introduces using AI to evaluate AI, noting AIs are about as good as humans at this task. Recommends using a better LLM for evaluation than for production, and mentions Galileo's custom-trained evaluation model.

sections.title: Fintech Chatbot Demo and the Need for Granularity
sections.summary: Walks through a fintech chatbot demo where account balance queries require multiple turns, illustrating the need for step-level evaluation granularity and for integrating evaluations from day one through production.

sections.title: Evaluation Metrics: Action Completion and Action Advancement
sections.summary: Introduces action completion (did it achieve the end goal?) and action advancement (did it move forward?) metrics, showing how traces broken down by individual steps with red/green indicators enable precise failure diagnosis.

sections.title: AI-Generated Insights and Suggested Fixes
sections.summary: Describes how placing an LLM over unstructured evaluation data generates smart insights and suggested fixes, such as recommending explicit system message instructions so the chatbot retrieves all account balances. Fixes are not applied automatically due to risk of cascading issues.

sections.title: Human-in-the-Loop and Continuous Learning by Human Feedback
sections.summary: Emphasizes that human-in-the-loop review is critical because AI-generated metrics may be wrong. Introduces CLHF (continuous learning by human feedback) for ongoing metric training, since metrics are never perfect out of the box.

sections.title: Steps to Tame AI Agents: Evaluations, Metrics, Production, Alerting
sections.summary: Provides a step-by-step recap: add evaluations from the start, define precise metrics at design time (toxicity, hallucinations, RAG, custom), carry through production since users behave unpredictably, and implement real-time alerting for rogue agents.

sections.title: Closing and Q&A Invitation
sections.summary: Bennett closes, identifies himself as Principal Developer Advocate at Galileo, invites attendees to visit the booth for more information and to sign up for the free offering, and opens the floor to questions.
